definitions.definition: In the Sants: the Lord beyond the three qualities and beyond form, image and incarnation, yet the object of love and remembrance ('nirguṇ rām'); not an abstraction to be merely known.
Dādū's Rām, formless and stainless (nirañjan), the one God of Hindu and Turk.

The Lord with qualities and form — the avatāras and the images of temple worship; for the Sants not the final object of devotion (Kabīr: the son of Daśaratha is praised, but the secret of Rām's name is other).

Loving devotion to the attributeless Lord through the Name, the guru and inner remembrance, without images or avatāras; the defining stance of the Sants (a scholarly label that the Sants' own 'nirguṇ rām' supports).
The Sants' most common name for the formless Lord who 'pervades every body' (ghaṭ ghaṭ rām) — explicitly distinguished from Rāma son of Daśaratha.
Rām as the nirguṇa object of remembrance of the 'lovers of Rām'.

cross_language.note: the Sanskrit name primarily denotes the avatāra

definitions.definition: 'The unseen, unmarked' — a name of the ultimate shared with Nāth usage ('alakh nirañjan'); in Sant Mat, Alakh Lok is a region above Sach Khand.
The stainless formless ultimate, the name of God for the Nirañjanīs, as for the Nāth yogīs ('alakh nirañjan').
The stainless one whom Dādū salutes first in his Vāṇī.
In the Dharamdāsī literature, Nirañjan is Kāl, the fallen creator of the three worlds (see trm:kal-niranjan).

equivalents.note: The same name is the highest for Nāths, Nirañjanīs and Dādū, and a lower, deceiving power for the Kabīr Panth and Sant Mat; see dsp:status-of-niranjan.

definitions.definition: The son of the Sat Puruṣ who by austerity won the three worlds, begot Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheś, and as Kāl (time/death) devours souls and keeps them from Satlok; the adversary from whom Kabīr frees souls.

Kāl, the 'negative power' (also Brahm, Jot Nirañjan at the lower levels), ruler of the three worlds up to Trikuṭī, the universal mind, who administers karma; contrasted with Dayāl, the merciful supreme.
Kāl as death, who stands over every head and grinds the world.
The True Being, supreme Lord of Satlok, from whom the sixteen sons emanated; Kabīr is his incarnation or messenger.
Sat Purush, the Lord of Sach Khand / Sat Lok, the first manifestation of the Supreme in the purely spiritual region.
The true world of the Sat Puruṣ beyond the three worlds of Kāl, the home to which freed souls (haṃs) return.
Sat Lok = Sach Khand, the fifth region, the true home of the soul beyond the reach of Kāl and māyā.
The world Kabīr showed Garībdās.

equivalents.note: Sant Mat itself identifies Sat Lok with Sach Khand.
Same name as the Purāṇic highest world of Brahmā, but the Kabīr Panth places Satlok beyond all worlds of Kāl, including Brahmā's.

definitions.definition: The 'true region', the fifth inner region reached by the soul on the sound current, where it meets the Sat Purush; beyond it Alakh, Agam and Anāmī.
The 'nameless', the highest region and the supreme being beyond all names, which Radhasoami calls Radhasoami Dhām.
The true name of the supreme being and of the highest region, revealed by Soamiji; glossed in the Agra literature as Rādhā (the soul/current) and Soamī (the Lord).
The 'merciful' — the supreme spiritual power of the pure regions, opposed to Kāl, the negative power; Dayāl Deś is the pure spiritual region above Kāl's domain.
The will or pleasure of the Supreme (and of the Master), to which the disciple surrenders; everything happens by the Mauj.
The 'true name' of the formless Lord, the centre of Satnāmī devotion and the source of the movements' name.
The true Name given at initiation by which the soul passes Kāl.
The 'city without sorrow' of Ravidās's song: no grief, tax, fear or ranks; the goal and the ideal community of the Ravidāsīs.
The Name of the Lord (usually Rām), whose inward remembrance is the Sants' chief practice; not the spoken syllables only but the Name revealed by the guru and dwelt on with the mind.
Nām = Śabd: the creative Word, the inner sound and light, to which the names given at initiation connect the soul; distinguished from 'varṇātmak' (spoken) names.
The true Name (sat nām) given at initiation with the pān-parvānā, by which the soul passes Kāl.
The Word: the guru's word that awakens the disciple, and the inner Word/sound by which the Lord is known; also the name of the song genre (śabda, pad).
Shabd, the audible life stream or sound current — the creative power of the Supreme, heard within and followed back to its source.
The unstruck sound (anhad nād, anhad bājā) heard within in the encounter with the Lord; a Nāth-derived image used by Kabīr and Dādū.
The inner sound heard in meditation, distinguished into the sounds of the successive regions.
The sound or melody of the Word heard within; 'Shabd dhun' is the sound current.
The inner light seen without sun or moon in the encounter with the Lord; Kabīr's first ramainī places light and sound at the origin.
The light of the inner regions (the flame at Sahasdal Kanwal, 'Jot Nirañjan'); the soul follows the sound and sees the light.
Remembrance of the Name, inward and constant, with the breath; repetition on beads without the mind is not sumiran.
Simran: mental repetition of the names given at initiation, to gather the attention at the eye centre.
'Unrepeated repetition': the Name going on by itself with the breath, without tongue or beads (Dādū, Kabīr and the Nāth-influenced Sants).
The soul as attention or consciousness-current, a drop of the Supreme scattered through the body; it is gathered at the eye centre and rises on the sound current (surat-śabd).
In Kabīr and the Nāth-influenced Sants: attention or recollection fixed on the Lord (surati-nirati).

equivalents.note: Sant Mat's surat is the individual soul considered as a current of attention.

definitions.definition: The seeing faculty of the soul, paired with surat (hearing faculty): surat hears the sound, nirat sees the light.
In Kabīr: absorption or detachment paired with surati.
The freed soul, a swan that returns to Satlok when it receives the true Name; Kāl's prey is the crow, the Name makes it a swan.
The soul as a swan that feeds on pearls (the Name) at the Mānasarovar within.
The 'tenth door' at the crown of the head beyond the nine bodily openings, through which the soul goes out to the Lord; Nāth-derived image in Kabīr and Dādū.
Daswān Dwār: the third region above Trikuṭī (also called Sunn), where the soul, free of mind and matter, sees itself as pure spirit.

equivalents.note: Both name an opening at the crown; the Sant Mat Daswān Dwār is a region, not only an aperture.

definitions.definition: The 'sky-circle' in the head where nectar drips, light shines and the unstruck sound is heard; Nāth-derived image in Kabīr and Dādū.

equivalents.note: Both name the highest centre in the head; the Sant image is not systematized as a lotus.

definitions.definition: The second inner region ('three prominences'), seat of Brahm/the universal mind and source of the Veda, sounding like thunder or drum; the causal region.
In Kabīr and the Nāth-influenced Sants, the meeting place between the brows (trikuṭī) where Gaṅgā, Yamunā and Sarasvatī meet.
The thousand-petalled lotus, the first inner region above the eye centre, seat of Jot Nirañjan, where the bell and conch sound and a flame is seen.

cross_language.note: in haṭha texts the crown lotus (sahasrāra); in Sant Mat the first region above the eyes

definitions.definition: The 'whirling cave', the fourth region above Mahāsunn, where the flute is heard.
The 'third eye' or eye centre behind and between the eyebrows, where the scattered attention is gathered by simran and the inner journey begins.

equivalents.note: Located at the brow like the ājñā cakra, but Sant Mat places it above the six lower cakras as the door out of the body.

definitions.definition: The body as 'pot' or vessel in which the Lord dwells ('ghaṭ ghaṭ rām'); the site of the search.
'Gift of the Name': initiation by the living Master, with the names for simran and instruction in dhyān and bhajan.
Devotional song and worship; the Sants' songs are sung as bhajan in satsaṅg.
In Sant Mat also the technical name of listening to the inner sound current.
'Witness': the rhymed couplet (dohā) in which the Sants bear witness to what they have seen; arranged in aṅgas.

cross_language.note: the sense 'witness' carried into the genre name

definitions.definition: A verse form (caupāī stanzas closed by a sākhī) used for doctrine, especially cosmology, in the Bījak.
'Limb' or topic: a chapter of a Sant anthology gathering sākhīs on one theme (gurudev kau aṅg, birah kau aṅg …).
The 'utterance' of a saint — his or her collected words, treated as scripture by the panth.
'Upside-down speech': riddling songs of impossible images (the lion grazing cows, the son born before the mother) whose inversion points to the reversal of ordinary perception.

equivalents.note: Both are coded, paradoxical registers; the Sant form is a genre of songs, the Buddhist/Bāul form a language of double meanings.

definitions.definition: The 'twilight' or intentional language of double meanings in which Bāul songs speak of body practice and the Man of the Heart, so that the uninitiated hear only devotional or everyday words.
The coded language of the Sahajiyā manuals and padas.

notes: The term itself comes from the Buddhist tantric commentarial tradition (Caryāgīti; owned by U44).

definitions.definition: Discernment, assaying (as a jeweller tests a gem): the Bījak's key virtue of testing every doctrine and deity as the mind's creation; the basis of the 'Pārakh' school of Bījak interpretation.
'Acquaintance': the direct encounter with the Lord (paracā kau aṅg); also the genre of hagiography that makes a saint known (paracaī).
The pain of separation from the Beloved, praised as 'the sultan' and as the sign of true devotion; the body without it is a cremation ground.
The longing for the Man of the Heart who comes near and cannot be held.
'Dead while living': the devotee who has let the self, hope and pride die while still alive; death has nothing left to take.
Dying while living: daily withdrawal of the attention from the body to the eye centre as at death.
jyānte marā: the lover who has died to lust and self while alive.

equivalents.note: Both describe freedom in the living body; the Sant term stresses the death of the self rather than the dawning of knowledge.

definitions.definition: The natural, innate state: the Lord realized without forced austerities, with eyes open, every act worship; 'sahaj samādhi'. Kabīr also warns that all speak of sahaj and none knows it.
The innate: the ultimate nature of man and woman as Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā and the state of union beyond the two; the goal of the Sahajiyā path.
The natural Man and the natural way (sahaj mānuṣ, sahaj pathe) found in the body under the guru.
The sahaja mānuṣa, the Master hidden in the human, and the sahaja religion revealed by Āulcānd.

cross_language.note: the Buddhist Sahajiyā sense (the innate as the union of wisdom and means), see U44

definitions.definition: Natural absorption: absorption without closing the eyes, stopping the ears or torturing the body, in which walking is circumambulation and lying down prostration.
The 'no-mind' state beyond the mind, a Nāth term used by Kabīr for absorption in the Lord.
The void or empty sky (sunn, śūnya-maṇḍal) in the head where the Lord is met — a Nāth-derived name for the highest state, not a Buddhist emptiness.
Sunn (with Mahāsunn above it): the region of the soul's self-realization above Trikuṭī, where the sārangī is heard.
The round of 8.4 million species of birth through which the soul wanders; the human birth, rare within it, is the only chance to be freed.
The true guru who gives the Name and the Word and opens the inner eye; praised equal to or above God (guru and Govind).
The Sant Satguru: a living master who has reached the highest region and is its embodiment; indispensable for initiation and inner guidance.

equivalents.note: The Sant satguru is the guru who reveals the Name within; outward family or sect gurus are not satgurus.

definitions.definition: The living guru (also murśid, sāṃi) through whom alone the Man of the Heart is found; Bāuls distinguish the initiating guru (dīkṣā-guru) and the instructing guru (śikṣā-guru).
The Mahāśay, in whom the Kartā is present; 'the guru is truth'.
A holy person who has realized the Truth (sat) and lives by it — used by the tradition for its poet-saints and for any true sādhu; in Sant Mat, a master who has reached the highest region.
The company of sants and gathering to sing and hear their words; the purifying association without which the Name does not take root.
The Master's discourse and the gathering of disciples; also, inwardly, contact with the Word.
'Path': an organized following of a Sant (Kabīr Panth, Dādū Panth), with initiation, seats and sādhus — which the Sants' own verses often warn against making sectarian.
The bead necklace (of tulsī wood) given at initiation into the Kabīr Panth (and Dādū Panth).
The consecrated betel-leaf 'passport' given in the Dharamdāsī initiation and death rites, which Kāl's messengers honour.
The square ritual ground and rite (caukā āratī) of the Dharamdāsī Kabīr Panth, performed for initiation and for the dead, with coconut, betel and lamps.
'Without a side': Dādū's impartiality, belonging neither to Hindu nor Turk.
The 'avadhū' whom Kabīr addresses in many songs — the Nāth yogī, challenged to find the Lord within rather than in yogic garb and feats.
Direct experience of the Lord, set against book-learning ('I speak of what I have seen with my eyes'); aṇbhai vāṇī is speech from such experience.

The great swindler (mahāṭhaginī) with the noose of the three qualities, who takes a different form in every house (Lakṣmī, Bhavānī, idol, pilgrim-water) and binds the world; also 'gold and woman' (kanak-kāminī).
Māyā, the material power ruling the lower regions under Kāl.
The mind: restless elephant, thief and bird, the seat of both defeat and victory; it must be tamed by the guru's word and remembrance, for the Name recited while the mind wanders is useless.
The mind is the agent of Kāl, attached to the soul; it is left behind at Trikuṭī/Daswān Dwār.
Man: the mind or heart, addressed in the songs ('o my mind'); also the seat of the Man of the Heart (maner mānuṣ).
Delusion — above all the sectarian delusions of Hindu and Turk and the belief in outward means; 'bhram bidhauṃsaṇ' is its destruction.
The sectarian garb and marks of ascetics (ochre, matted locks, earrings, beads, ash), which the Sants reject as display.
Religious hypocrisy and empty show; Viśvanāth Siṃh's Bījak commentary is 'the destroyer of pākhaṇḍ'.
Birth-group or caste, which the Sants declare has no standing before God ('do not ask a sādhu's caste').
Jāt: caste and creed; Lalon has 'never seen its form' and asks where it is at birth and death.
Pilgrim place; the Sants deny that bathing at tīrthas purifies — the true Gaṅgā is in a pure mind.
The pilgrimage is within: 'the original Mecca is in this human body'.
The incarnations come from the regions of Kāl to maintain order in the creation; the Saints come from the highest region to take souls home and are above them.
Kabīr's descents in the four ages are not avatāras of Viṣṇu but comings of the Sat Puruṣ's messenger; Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheś are Kāl's sons.
Of three kinds: pralabdh (destiny, lived out in this body), sinchit (stored, burnt by the Master and by practice) and kriyaman (new, avoided by the disciple's vows).
The destiny karma that made the present body; not altered by the Master, only borne with detachment.
The embodied soul, a part of the Lord who dwells in the same body unrecognized, like musk in the deer.
Sundardās: the one without a second, known at the end of the path as one's own self.
Brahm is the ruler of Trikuṭī and the universal mind, the highest god of the Vedas but within Kāl's domain; Pārbrahm is the region above it.
Grace received from the guru met in the unseen.
Parshād: food or grace blessed by the Master.
The nectar that rains in the sky-circle of the head in the encounter with the Lord; also the guru as 'mine of nectar'.
Voluntary service of the Master and the community (physical, financial, mental), a support of meditation.
Sādhu-sevā: feeding and serving the sādhus at melās and ākhṛās.
Seeing the Master, outwardly and within (the Radiant Form), which purifies and draws the soul.
In Bāul usage: inference, hearsay and scripture — everything not verifiable in the living body — set aside in favour of bartamān.
A 'madman' (of God): a practitioner who has abandoned convention to seek the Man of the Heart; the word appears in the Caitanya-caritāmṛta (Antya 19) for the God-mad.
The 'Man of the Heart': the divine dwelling in the human body, sought, longed for and met through the guru; also called the unknown bird, the uncatchable man, the neighbour in the mirror-city.

equivalents.note: The Bāul maner mānuṣ and the Sahajiyā sahaja mānuṣa name the same indwelling divine person in the two idioms.

definitions.definition: The innate Man, the divine as present in the human person (Kṛṣṇa in man, Rādhā in woman); 'the truth of man is above all'.
The natural Man within, to be worshipped in the human (mānuṣ bhajan).
The Master hidden in the human form, revealed by the Kartā.
The 'uncatchable Man', the Man of the Heart as he comes and goes in the body and slips from grasp; in coded songs he appears at a certain time 'with the tide'.
The 'unknown bird' that comes and goes in the cage of the body — the soul or the Man of the Heart.
The 'city of mirrors' near the house (the body), where the unseen neighbour (the Man) lives.
The 'truth of the body': Bāul body-theology, in which the body contains the cosmos, the gods and the Man, and is the only field of practice.
The Sahajiyā doctrine of the inner body with its lakes and lotuses as the eternal Vṛndāvana.
'Vessel and universe': 'what is in the vessel (body) is in the universe' — the correspondence of body and cosmos.

cross_language.note: cf. 'yat piṇḍe tat brahmāṇḍe' in Nāth and haṭha usage

definitions.definition: 'The present': what is here and now, verifiable in the living body; the Bāuls call themselves bartamān-panthī, followers of the present.

equivalents.note: Like perception, bartamān is direct knowledge, but it is specifically the body's own experience and is set against scripture as such.

definitions.definition: 'Reverse practice': turning the downward, outward flow (of desire and bodily substance) back upward and inward; recorded here as a doctrine only (restricted).
The Sahajiyā reversal by which kāma is turned into prema.

equivalents.note: Both describe an upward reversal of the vital substance; the Bāul form is a couple's practice and is framed devotionally.

definitions.definition: 'Upstream': going against the current, the direction of Bāul practice, as the fish swims upstream.

The 'four moons': coded name for four bodily substances whose secret handling under a guru belongs to Bāul body practice; recorded only as a name (restricted), with the tradition's warnings that it is secret and ruinous without a guru.

notes: RESTRICTED: no method or substance-handling details are recorded.

definitions.definition: Breath (Persian dam), as the vehicle on which the Man moves; the subject of coded breath practice (restricted, summary only).
Worship of the human: God is served and found in the human being, above all in the guru.
The Kartābhajā maxim 'worship the human'.
The Bāul hermitage or gathering place of a guru and disciples, where songs are sung and practice taught (e.g. Lalon's ākhṛā at Cheuṛiyā).

cross_language.note: among North Indian ascetics the word names an armed order or its seat

definitions.definition: Festival gathering of Bāuls and fakirs (Joydeb-Kenduli at Pauṣ Saṃkrānti; Lalon's festival at Cheuṛiyā), for singing, sādhu-sevā and teaching.
Taking the mendicant's garb: the Bāul initiation into renunciation (with the ālkhāllā robe), after the first initiation (dīkṣā).
Among Muslim Bāul-Fakirs: the initiation into renunciant fakirhood (the fakiri counterpart of bhek).
A mendicant; the self-designation of Muslim Bāuls and of Lalon's line ('Lalon Fakir').
'Master': title of a Bāul-Fakir guru (Lalon Sāṃi, Sirāj Sāṃi).
The guru (Arabic-Persian term) in Bāul-Fakir usage; Madan Bāul sings that guru and murśid stand in the way when they become institutions.
Gnosis: the fourth and inmost of the four ways (after śariyat, tarikat, hakikat) by which Bāul-Fakirs place their path beyond the law — recorded as context (Sufi vocabulary).
'Mad one': a name of affection for the God-mad Bāul.
The one-stringed drone instrument of the Bāul singer, a sign of the one Truth.
The outward human form of man and woman, onto which the divine nature (svarūpa) is superimposed in practice.
The inner divine nature of every person: Kṛṣṇa in the man, Rādhā in the woman.
Superimposition: attributing the svarūpa (Kṛṣṇa, Rādhā) to the rūpa of the practitioner and partner, the key contemplative act of Sahajiyā practice.
Desire for one's own pleasure, which is not destroyed but refined into prema by the Sahajiyā discipline, as gold from ore; the washerwoman's love had no trace of it.
Lust, the downward current that must be mastered before the Man can be held.
Love of the Lord — 'the two and a half letters of prem' worth more than all books; its lane is too narrow for two.
Selfless divine love, the goal of the siddha stage, refined out of kāma.
Prem: the love-practice (prem-sādhanā) of the one who has died while alive.
The essence of love tasted in the union of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, located in the Sahajiyā body; the Sahajiyā reads Rūpa Gosvāmī's rasa theory as a guide to embodied practice.
Love-feeling (and, in coded usage, its bodily basis) that the practitioner must stabilize and raise into prema.

Love for one who is not one's spouse, taken as the model of the practitioner's relation with the partner, because it is free of social motive and full of risk and longing — recorded in summary only (restricted context).
The supreme love of Rādhā, which the Sahajiyā sees embodied in Caitanya and attainable in the sahaja state of the couple.
The divine couple (Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa) and the human couple in which they are realized.
The beginner's stage, relying on the name and the guru's mantra.
The practitioner's stage, relying on bhāva.
The perfected stage, resting in prema and the sahaja state.
The woman partner of the Sahajiyā (and Bāul) practitioner, regarded as Rādhā and often as the guru of the practice; recorded without details (restricted context).

The 'nine connoisseurs' whom Sahajiyā tradition counts as its exemplary masters, each with a female partner (e.g. Caṇḍīdās and Rāmī, Jayadeva and Padmāvatī, Vidyāpati and Lachimā, Bilvamaṅgala and Cintāmaṇi); the list varies.

notes: Membership of the list recalled with low confidence.

definitions.definition: The 'Master' or 'Doer': God as the one Lord, present in Āulcānd and in the hereditary head (Kartā) of the sect; the Kartābhajā are 'worshippers of the Kartā'.
'Great-souled': a Kartābhajā guru who initiates and collects dues from the disciples (barātī).
A disciple of the Kartābhajā, who pays dues through a Mahāśay to the Kartā.
The 'true religion': the Kartābhajā self-designation for the sahaja teaching revealed by Āulcānd.
'Secret': the hidden core of the Kartābhajā teaching and the hidden presence of the Master, kept behind outward conformity.
